english: Tell me about it / I know, right? / Exactly what I was thinking (strong, sympathetic agreement)
usage: 그러게 말이에요, 저도 딱 그 생각 했어요.
Tell me about it — I was thinking the exact same thing.
Agreeing and confirming you felt it too
그러게 말이야, 진짜 너무하지 않아?
I know, right? Isn't it just too much?
그러게 말이야 = casual form with friends
그러게나 말이에요.
Yeah, you can say that again.
그러게나 = slightly stronger/heavier sigh
그러게 말입니다.
Indeed, you're quite right.
-ㅂ니다 form, polite to a senior or at work
examples: A: 요즘 물가가 너무 올랐어요. B: 그러게 말이에요, 장 보기가 무서워요.
A: Prices have shot up lately. B: Tell me about it, I'm scared to go grocery shopping.
Empathetic agreement + adding to the complaint
A: 주말마다 비가 오네요. B: 그러게 말이에요, 빨래를 못 하겠어요.
A: It rains every weekend. B: I know, right? I can't even do laundry.
Sharing a small frustration
A: 그 사람 진짜 일을 잘하더라고요. B: 그러게 말이에요, 저도 깜짝 놀랐어요.
A: That person is really good at their job. B: Right? I was surprised too.
Agreeing about a positive observation
nuance: Conversational, empathetic agreement — stronger than a plain 네 or 맞아요 because it adds 'and I feel exactly the same.' It usually comes with a shared sigh or nod, signaling you've had the same thought. Casual-polite as 그러게 말이에요; drop to 그러게 말이야 with close friends. Note it's the longer, more emphatic cousin of just 그러게요.
mistakes: It's for agreeing with the other person's remark, not for accepting praise about yourself.
Don't use it to introduce a new disagreement — it only confirms what was just said.

english: No, that's not it — / It's not that, it's… / What I mean is… (correcting a misunderstanding)
usage: 그게 아니라, 제 말은 좀 다른 뜻이었어요.
No, that's not it — what I meant was a bit different.
Clarifying after being misunderstood
아니 그게 아니라, 시간이 없어서 그래.
No no, it's not that — it's because I don't have time.
그게 아니라 = casual; correcting a wrong assumption
그런 게 아니라 그냥 좀 피곤해서요.
It's not like that, I'm just a bit tired.
그런 게 아니라 = 'it's not that kind of thing'
그게 아니고, 다시 설명할게요.
That's not it — let me explain again.
그게 아니고 = looser spoken variant
examples: A: 저 싫어서 안 오시는 거예요? B: 아, 그게 아니라 오늘 진짜 바빠서요.
A: Are you not coming because you don't like me? B: Oh, that's not it — I'm just really busy today.
Heading off a hurt feeling
A: 환불해 달라는 거죠? B: 그게 아니라 교환을 하고 싶어서요.
A: So you want a refund? B: No, it's that I'd like an exchange.
Correcting a misread request
그게 아니라요, 제가 주문한 건 아메리카노예요.
That's not right — what I ordered was an americano.
그게 아니라요 adds 요 for extra politeness
nuance: Everyday correction phrase used the moment someone misreads what you said or why you did something. Leading with 그게 아니라 softens the correction — you're fixing the misunderstanding, not arguing. Works in casual and polite speech; the 라 ending naturally connects to your real point, so always follow it with the correct version.
mistakes: It's a lead-in, not a complete sentence — attach your actual meaning after it.
Don't confuse 그게 아니라 (correcting a misunderstanding) with 그게 아니면 ('if not that, then…'), which offers an alternative.

english: Now that you mention it / Come to think of it / Now that I think about it (realizing something mid-conversation)
usage: 그러고 보니 오늘 점심을 안 먹었네요.
Come to think of it, I haven't eaten lunch today.
Realizing something as you speak
그러고 보니까 너 머리 잘랐네?
Now that I look — did you get a haircut?
그러고 보니까 = -까 adds a casual 'now that…'
그러고 보니 벌써 12월이네요.
Now that you mention it, it's already December.
Noticing how time has passed
듣고 보니 그러네요.
Now that I hear it, you're right.
Related: 듣고 보니 = 'now that I've heard it'
examples: A: 민수 씨 요즘 안 보이네요. B: 그러고 보니 진짜 한참 못 봤네요.
A: I haven't seen Minsu lately. B: Now that you mention it, it really has been a while.
Triggered by the other person's remark
그러고 보니 우산을 카페에 두고 왔어요.
Come to think of it, I left my umbrella at the cafe.
Suddenly remembering something
그러고 보니 우리 처음 만난 지 벌써 일 년 됐네요.
Now that I think about it, it's already been a year since we first met.
Reflecting on the passage of time
nuance: Casual-polite connector for the moment a thought clicks into place — often sparked by what the other person just said, or by glancing at something. It literally means 'looking at it that way,' and flags that you're noticing something you'd overlooked. Same form in casual and polite speech; just adjust the verb ending that follows.
mistakes: Don't use it for things you already knew — it specifically marks a fresh realization.
Keep the spacing 그러고 보니 (two words); 그리고 ('and') is a different word entirely.

english: Maybe that's why / Perhaps because of that / That might be why (guessing a cause)
usage: 어제 잠을 못 잤어요. 그래서 그런지 하루 종일 피곤하네요.
I couldn't sleep last night. Maybe that's why I'm tired all day.
Linking a likely cause to a result
주말이라 그런지 사람이 진짜 많네.
Maybe because it's the weekend, there are so many people.
N(이)라 그런지 = 'perhaps because it's N'
비가 와서 그런지 길이 한산해요.
Perhaps because it's raining, the streets are quiet.
V/A-아서 그런지 = 'maybe because ~'
요즘 운동을 해서 그런지 컨디션이 좋아요.
Maybe it's because I've been exercising — I feel great lately.
Crediting a habit for a good result
examples: A: 오늘따라 가게가 한가하네요. B: 평일이라 그런지 손님이 별로 없어요.
A: The shop's unusually quiet today. B: Maybe because it's a weekday, there aren't many customers.
Speculating about a cause
새 안경을 써서 그런지 눈이 좀 피곤해요.
Maybe because I'm wearing new glasses, my eyes feel tired.
Tentative self-diagnosis
겨울이라 그런지 해가 빨리 지네요.
Perhaps because it's winter, the sun sets fast.
Soft explanation, not a firm claim
nuance: Soft, speculative connector meaning 'I'm guessing this is the reason.' The -ㄴ지 ending keeps it tentative, so you sound observant rather than certain — very natural when you're not 100% sure of the cause. Use 그래서 그런지 to refer back to a reason you just stated, or attach -아서/어서 그런지 or -(이)라 그런지 directly to the cause.
mistakes: For a definite cause use 그래서 ('so/therefore'); 그래서 그런지 always carries a 'maybe' hedge.
It links a cause to an observed result — don't use it to give commands or make requests.

english: Anyway / By the way / That aside (changing the subject)
usage: 그건 그렇고, 점심 뭐 먹을까요?
Anyway, what should we eat for lunch?
Pivoting to a new topic
그건 그렇고 너 요즘 회사는 어때?
By the way, how's work these days?
Casual subject change with a friend
그건 그렇다 치고, 다음 얘기 해요.
Setting that aside, let's move on.
그건 그렇다 치고 = 'granting that, anyway'
그나저나 시간 괜찮으세요?
Anyway, do you have time?
그나저나 = a close synonym for switching topics
examples: A: 그 드라마 결말이 좀 아쉬웠어요. B: 그러게요. 그건 그렇고, 주말에 시간 돼요?
A: That drama's ending was a bit disappointing. B: Right. Anyway, are you free this weekend?
Wrapping one topic to start another
회의는 잘 끝났어요. 그건 그렇고, 점심 같이 하실래요?
The meeting went fine. By the way, want to grab lunch together?
Smoothly shifting at work
그건 그렇고, 아까 말한 그 책 제목이 뭐였죠?
Anyway, what was the title of that book you mentioned earlier?
Returning to or opening a new thread
nuance: Friendly topic-switcher literally meaning 'that's that, and…' — it gently closes the current subject and opens a new one. It signals 'enough about this, moving on,' without sounding abrupt. Casual-polite and very common in conversation; 그나저나 is an interchangeable alternative.
mistakes: Don't use it to disagree — it changes topics, it doesn't push back on what was said.
Keep the spacing 그건 그렇고; 그건 = 그것은 contracted.

english: Since we're on the subject / Now that it's come up / Speaking of which (segueing into a related point)
usage: 말이 나왔으니까 하는 말인데, 저도 그게 좀 불편했어요.
Since it's come up, I'll say it — that bothered me a little too.
말이 나왔으니까 하는 말인데 = set lead-in to a frank remark
말 나온 김에 지금 정하자.
Since we're already on it, let's decide now.
말 나온 김에 = shorter, casual variant
여행 말이 나왔으니까 말인데, 다음에 같이 갈래요?
Speaking of travel — want to go together next time?
Tacking onto a topic that just arose
돈 얘기가 나왔으니까 솔직히 말할게요.
Since money came up, I'll be honest.
얘기가 나왔으니까 = 'since the talk came up'
examples: A: 회식은 다음 주 금요일이에요. B: 아, 말이 나왔으니까, 저는 그날 좀 늦을 것 같아요.
A: The team dinner is next Friday. B: Oh, since it's come up — I'll probably be a bit late that day.
Adding relevant info while the topic is open
말이 나왔으니까 하는 말인데, 그 집 음식 별로였어요.
Since we're talking about it — that place's food wasn't great.
Easing into an honest opinion
이사 말이 나왔으니까 말인데, 좋은 집 있으면 소개해 줘요.
Speaking of moving — if you know a good place, let me know.
Riding a topic into a small request
nuance: Spoken segue that piggybacks on a topic someone just raised, so your follow-up feels natural rather than out of the blue. The fuller 말이 나왔으니까 하는 말인데 ('since it came up, here's what I'll say') often precedes a candid remark or request. Casual-polite; shorten to 말 나온 김에 with friends.
mistakes: Use it only when the topic genuinely just came up; to switch to an unrelated topic, use 그건 그렇고.
It's a lead-in — follow it with the actual point you want to add.

english: Oh good / What a relief / I'm glad to hear that (relieved that things turned out okay)
usage: 다 잘 끝났다니 다행이네요.
I'm glad to hear it all worked out.
Reacting with relief to good news
안 다쳤다니 정말 다행이다.
Thank goodness you weren't hurt.
다행이다 = casual; 정말 adds weight
불행 중 다행이에요.
It's a blessing in disguise / could've been worse.
불행 중 다행 = set phrase, 'fortunate amid misfortune'
늦지 않아서 다행이에요.
Good thing we weren't late.
V/A-아서 다행이다 = 'lucky that ~'
examples: A: 검사 결과 괜찮대요. B: 아, 다행이네요. 걱정 많이 했어요.
A: The test results are fine. B: Oh, what a relief. I was so worried.
Relief after worrying news
A: 지갑 잃어버린 줄 알았는데 가방에 있었어요. B: 다행이네요!
A: I thought I lost my wallet, but it was in my bag. B: Oh good!
Reacting to a near-miss
비가 그쳐서 다행이에요, 우산이 없었거든요.
Good thing the rain stopped — I didn't have an umbrella.
Expressing personal relief
nuance: Warm, genuine reaction expressing relief — 다행 means 'good fortune,' so it's 'how fortunate.' Said to others it reads as caring ('I'm relieved for you'); about your own situation it's 'phew.' Casual-polite as 다행이네요/다행이에요; drop to 다행이다 with friends. The -네요 adds a touch of heartfelt spontaneity.
mistakes: Spelling is 다행 (多幸); don't write 다행히 here — 다행히 is the adverb 'fortunately.'
It's about relief, not congratulations; for an achievement use 축하해요 instead.

english: Oh no, this is bad / We're in trouble / Uh-oh, big problem (reacting to something going wrong)
usage: 큰일 났다, 지갑을 집에 두고 왔어.
Oh no, I left my wallet at home.
Realizing a problem; casual
어떡해요, 큰일 났어요.
What do I do, this is a disaster.
큰일 났어요 = polite; pairs with 어떡해요
이러다 큰일 나겠다.
At this rate something bad's going to happen.
큰일 나다 (future) = 'trouble will happen'
큰일 날 뻔했어요.
That was a close call — could've been a disaster.
큰일 날 뻔하다 = 'nearly went wrong'
examples: 큰일 났다, 발표 자료를 안 가져왔어.
Oh no, I didn't bring the presentation file.
Sudden realization of a mistake
A: 기차 막차 끊겼대요. B: 헐, 큰일 났네요.
A: They say the last train's gone. B: Oh no, we're in trouble.
Reacting to bad news together
이번 달에도 적자면 진짜 큰일 나요.
If we're in the red again this month, we're really in trouble.
Warning about a serious consequence
nuance: High-alarm reaction literally meaning 'a big thing has happened' — said when you realize something's gone wrong or is about to. Tone ranges from genuine panic to a half-joking 'uh-oh.' 큰일 났다/났어 with friends, 큰일 났어요 in polite speech; 큰일 나다 in future/conditional warns of looming trouble. Often paired with 어떡해 ('what do I do').
mistakes: Keep the spacing 큰일 났다 (큰일 is one noun).
Don't use it for minor inconveniences; it implies a real problem (even if exaggerated for effect).

english: Oh no, what to do / Oh dear / How awful (sympathetic worry, often on someone's behalf)
usage: 아이고, 어쩌나.
Oh dear, what to do.
아이고 + 어쩌나 = classic worried reaction
이를 어쩌나, 표가 다 매진이네.
Oh no, what now — the tickets are all sold out.
이를 어쩌나 = 'what to do about this'
어쩌나 했는데 잘 풀렸어요.
I was worried, but it sorted itself out.
어쩌나 했는데 = 'I was anxious, but…'
혼자 가야 한다니 어쩌니.
You have to go alone? Oh dear.
어쩌니 = softer/older-sounding variant
examples: A: 감기가 안 낫네요. B: 어쩌나, 병원은 가 보셨어요?
A: My cold won't go away. B: Oh no — have you seen a doctor?
Sympathetic concern for someone
짐이 이렇게 많은데 비까지 오니 어쩌나.
So much luggage and now it's raining too — what to do.
Worrying about a tough situation
면접에 늦으면 어쩌나 조마조마했어요.
I was on edge, worried about being late to the interview.
어쩌나 inside a clause = 'worried that ~'
nuance: Soft exclamation of worry or sympathy — 'oh dear, what's to be done.' It's gentler and more tender than 큰일 났다, often directed at someone else's predicament, and warm rather than panicked. It can stand alone as a reaction or sit inside a sentence ('worried that…'). Slightly soft/caring in tone; 어쩌지 is a near-synonym for your own dilemma.
mistakes: It expresses concern, not blame — don't aim it at someone as criticism.
Standalone 어쩌나 is a feeling, not a real question; if you actually want advice, ask 어떻게 하죠?

english: That can happen / It's possible, I guess / Fair enough (accepting something as understandable)
usage: 뭐, 그럴 수도 있죠.
Well, that can happen, I suppose.
Accepting something gracefully
그럴 수도 있지, 누구나 실수하잖아.
That can happen — everyone makes mistakes.
그럴 수도 있지 = casual, reassuring
바쁘면 그럴 수도 있어요.
If you're busy, that's understandable.
Excusing someone's lapse
그럴 수도 있겠네요.
I suppose that could be the case.
Conceding a point as plausible
examples: A: 제가 깜빡하고 답장을 안 했어요. B: 괜찮아요, 그럴 수도 있죠.
A: I forgot to reply. B: It's okay, that happens.
Letting a small slip go
A: 그 사람이 오해했나 봐요. B: 그럴 수도 있죠, 설명이 부족했으니까요.
A: I think they misunderstood. B: That's possible — the explanation was lacking.
Conceding a reasonable point
처음이라 긴장했어요. 그럴 수도 있죠, 뭐.
I was nervous since it was my first time. That's only natural, I guess.
Trailing 뭐 adds an easygoing shrug
nuance: Easygoing, accepting phrase meaning 'that's within the realm of normal — no big deal.' Use it to forgive a minor mistake, validate someone's feeling, or concede that a possibility is reasonable. The -죠 ending invites soft mutual agreement. Casual-polite; 그럴 수도 있지 with friends. Generous in tone, the opposite of 말도 안 돼요.
mistakes: Don't use it to dismiss something serious — it signals 'understandable,' so it can sound flippant about a real problem.
그럴 수도 있죠 (accepting it happened) differs from 그럴 리가 없죠 ('no way that's true').

english: I think that'd be best / You'd better do that / That sounds like the way to go (gently recommending)
usage: 네, 그러는 게 좋겠어요.
Yes, I think that'd be best.
Agreeing that a suggested course is wise
피곤하면 좀 쉬는 게 좋겠어.
If you're tired, you'd better rest a bit.
V-는 게 좋겠다 = 'had better ~'; casual
미리 예약하는 게 좋겠어요.
It'd be best to book in advance.
Recommending a sensible step
그러지 않는 게 좋겠어요.
I don't think you should do that.
Negative form = gentle 'better not'
examples: A: 비도 오는데 그냥 집에 있을까요? B: 네, 그러는 게 좋겠어요.
A: It's raining — should we just stay home? B: Yes, I think that'd be best.
Endorsing the other person's idea
A: 의사한테 한번 물어볼까요? B: 그러는 게 좋겠어요.
A: Should I ask the doctor? B: That'd be the way to go.
Encouraging a wise action
오늘은 일찍 자는 게 좋겠어요, 내일 일찍 일어나야 하니까요.
You'd better sleep early today, since you have to get up early tomorrow.
Caring advice with a reason
nuance: Polite, gentle recommendation — V-는 게 좋겠다 literally 'it'd be good if (you/we) did ~,' i.e., 'had better.' The -겠- makes it a soft suggestion rather than an order, so it advises without bossing. 그러는 게 좋겠어요 specifically endorses a course already on the table ('yes, let's do that'). Casual as 그러는 게 좋겠어.
mistakes: It's advice, not a command — for a firm instruction use V-(으)세요.
Spacing: 그러는 게 (게 = 것이 contracted), written as a separate word.

english: Do as you like / Suit yourself / It's up to you (giving free rein — or, with a cold tone, 'fine, whatever')
usage: 편하실 대로 마음대로 하세요.
Please do whatever's comfortable for you.
Warm version — genuinely leaving it to them
네 마음대로 해.
Do whatever you want.
마음대로 해 = casual; tone decides if it's kind or curt
마음껏 드세요.
Help yourself, eat as much as you like.
마음껏 = 'to your heart's content' (friendly cousin)
그럼 마음대로 하든가.
Then do whatever you want, see if I care.
-든가 makes it pointedly cold/annoyed
examples: A: 여기 앉아도 돼요? B: 그럼요, 마음대로 하세요.
A: Can I sit here? B: Of course, make yourself at home.
Friendly, welcoming use
메뉴는 마음대로 고르세요, 제가 살게요.
Order whatever you like — it's on me.
Generously leaving the choice to them
A: 그냥 내 방식대로 할게요. B: …마음대로 하세요.
A: I'll just do it my way. B: …Suit yourself.
Cold, resigned tone — passive-aggressive
nuance: Means 'do it however you wish' (마음 = mind/heart, -대로 = 'in accordance with'). Tone is everything: said warmly it's generous ('go right ahead, no need to ask'); said flatly or with a sigh it turns into a frosty 'fine, do what you want, I give up.' Casual-polite as 마음대로 하세요; 마음대로 해 with friends. The friendly 마음껏 ('to your heart's content') never carries the cold edge.
mistakes: Be careful with tone — to a senior or in tension it can sound dismissive or rude.
Spelling: 마음대로 (one word, no space before 대로); don't write 맘대로 in formal contexts (it's a casual contraction).
